► Why efficiency matters?

Modern language models are powerful but resource-intensive

  • GPT-3 (175B): 650Gb memory
  • LLaMA-2 (70B): 260Gb memory
  • DistilBERT (66M): 251Mb memory

Challenges

  1. Training: Full fine-tuning is expensive (memory, compute, time)
    • Limits experimentation and iteration
    • Requires expensive GPUs
    • Slow to adapt to new tasks
  2. Deployment: Large models don't fit on edge devices
    • Mobile phones have ~4-8GB RAM
    • Cloud inference costs scale with model size
  3. Inference: Slow and costly at scale
    • User experience suffers from latency
    • Operating costs grow linearly with traffic
    • Energy consumption and environmental impact

Adaptation: Finetuning & Parameter-Efficient Methods

Adaptation: Finetuning & Parameter-Efficient Methods

Full Model Finetuning

Adaptation: Finetuning & Parameter-Efficient Methods ► Why Adapt Pre-trained Models?
  • Pre-trained LLMs have general language knowledge
    (and partial task knowledge through instruction tuning)
  • Task-specific adaptation improves performance
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide 6
Adaptation: Finetuning & Parameter-Efficient Methods ► Full Model Finetuning
Full Finetuning
Update all model parameters on task-specific data
  • Direct finetuning strategies
    • Continue training with task-specific data
    • Use lower learning rate than pre-training
  • Controlling finetuning
    Parameter freezing
    keep some layers fixed
    Layer-wise learning rates
    different rates per layer
    Gradual unfreezing
    unfreeze layers progressively
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide 7
Adaptation: Finetuning & Parameter-Efficient Methods ► Catastrophic Forgetting
Catastrophic Forgetting
Model loses pre-trained knowledge when finetuned on specific tasks
  • Causes
    • Aggressive parameter updates
    • Distribution shift between pre-training and finetuning
    • Limited task-specific data
  • Mitigation strategies
    • Lower learning rates and careful scheduling
    • Regularization (e.g. L2)
      L2 regularization should not be used on bias and normalization layers
    • Replay methods: mix pre-training and task data
      e.g. keeping MLM loss
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide 8
Adaptation: Finetuning & Parameter-Efficient Methods ► Learning Rate Scheduling
Learning Rate Scheduling
Adjust learning rate during training to improve convergence and prevent catastrophic forgetting
  • Warmup prevents early instability
  • Decay allows fine-grained optimization near convergence
  • Typical max LR: 1e−5 to 5e−5 (vs 1e−4 for pre-training)

There are many techniques

Linear warmup + decay
Gradually increase LR, then linearly decrease to 0
Cosine annealing
Smooth decay following cosine curve
Constant with warmup
Warmup then fixed LR (common in instruction tuning)
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide 9
Adaptation: Finetuning & Parameter-Efficient Methods ► Layer Freezing
Layer Freezing
Freeze (don't update) certain layers during finetuning, train only unfrozen layers
  • Basic approach
    • Freeze early layers (general features), train later layers (task-specific features)
    • In NLP: freeze embedding + early transformer layers
  • Motivation
    • Earlier layers learn general features, later layers learn specific features
    • Reduce compute and memory (no gradients for frozen layers)
    • Prevent catastrophic forgetting of general knowledge
    • Effective when limited task-specific data
  • Limitations
    • Less flexible than full finetuning
    • Need to decide which layers to freeze (manual tuning)
    • May underperform full finetuning on complex tasks
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide 10
► Gradual Unfreezing & Discriminative Learning
  1. Gradual Unfreezing
    • Start with all layers frozen except last layer
    • Train for N steps, then unfreeze next layer (last to first layers)
  2. Discriminative (layer-wise) learning rates
    Lower LR for early layers, higher LR for later layers: ηl=ηL×αL−l with α∈[0.9,0.95]
ULMFit Combines the various above tricks
Universal Language Model Fine-tuning for Text Classification:
2018. http://arxiv.org/abs/1801.06146.
  1. Pre-train → freeze all → unfreeze last → unfreeze next → ... → finetune all
  2. State-of-art for NLP before modern PEFT (2018)
  3. Foundation for many transfer learning practices
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3

Adaptation: Finetuning & Parameter-Efficient Methods

Parameter-Efficient Finetuning (PEFT)

► Parameter-Efficient Finetuning (PEFT)
Goal
Adapt models while updating only a small fraction of parameters
  • Benefits
    • Drastically reduced memory requirements
    • Faster training
    • Easy to store/deploy multiple task-specific models
    • Often comparable performance to full finetuning
  • Key approaches
    • Adapters (LoRA, Prefix tuning, IA³), Prompt tuning
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Adapters
Adapters
Small modules inserted into a transformer
Houlsby's adapters
Houlsby, N. et al.
2019. Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP.
Small bottleneck modules inserted between transformer layers
  • Down-projection: d→r (bottleneck dimension)
  • Non-linearity (e.g., ReLU)
  • Up-projection: r→d
  • Residual connection
  • Training
    • Freeze transformer parameters
    • Train only adapter parameters
    • Typical: 1-5% of total parameters
  • Advantages
    • Modular: swap adapters for different tasks
    • Minimal inference overhead
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation
LoRA
LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models:
2021. http://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685.
Hypothesis: weight updates lie in low-rank subspace
Add learnable low-rank matrices to existing weights
Represent weight updates as low-rank decomposition: ΔW=BA where B∈Rd×r, A∈Rr×k, r≪min(d,k)

Properties

  • Train only A and B (typically r=4 to 64)
  • No inference latency: merge W0+BA after training
  • Apply to attention weights (Q, K, V, O) or FFN
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► LORA variants

QLoRA

QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs:
2023. http://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314.
combine with quantization (4-bit base model)

DoRA

Liu, S.-Y. et al.
2024. DoRA: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation. Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning.
Decompose into magnitude and direction
Uses LORA for learning the direction
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► IA³: Infused Adapter by Inhibiting and Amplifying
IA³
Liu, H. et al.
2022. Few-Shot Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning Is Better and Cheaper than In-Context Learning. 36th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2022).
Learn element-wise scaling vectors that modulate activations
h=lk⊙Wkx (where ⊙ is element-wise product)
Even fewer parameters than LoRA (typically 0.01% of model)
No added inference latency
Rescaling is cheap computationally
More constrained than LoRA
May underperform on complex tasks
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Prompt Tuning

Inspiration: hard prompts

Direct model instruction
Example: "Translate to French:"
interpretable
not optimal
Prompt Tuning
Lester, B. et al.
2021. The Power of Scale for Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning. Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing.
Learn continuous "soft prompt" embeddings (20-100 "soft" tokens) prepended to the input
  • Add learnable embeddings to input: [esoft;einput]
  • Only affects first layer
  • Model processes soft prompt like regular tokens
Can match full finetuning on many tasks (with large models)
More effective as models grow (>10B params)
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Prefix Tuning
Prefix Tuning
Li, X.L. and Liang, P.
2021. Prefix-Tuning: Optimizing Continuous Prompts for Generation.
Prepend v learnable "virtual tokens" to each layer's key and value projections
x1:v(ℓ) are parameters of the model
in the paper, the authors use an MLP to predict the prefix (stabilizes the training)
More expressive than prompt tuning (affects all layers)
Can be sensitive to initialization
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► PEFT Methods Comparison

By parameter efficiency (fewest to most)

  1. Prompt Tuning: ~0.01% (input embeddings only)
  2. IA³: ~0.01% (scaling vectors)
  3. Prefix Tuning: ~0.1% (prefix vectors per layer)
  4. LoRA: ~0.1-1% (low-rank matrices)
  5. Adapters: ~1-5% (bottleneck layers)

Practical recommendations

  • LoRA: best default choice (balance of efficiency & performance)
  • Prompt/Prefix: very large models (>10B), trained with instruction tuning
  • IA³: extreme parameter constraints (very small datasets)

► The Inference Challenge
  • Problem
    • LLMs are huge: billions to trillions of parameters
    • Inference is slow and memory-intensive
    • Deployment costs are prohibitive
  • Optimization goals
    • Reduce memory footprint
    • Increase throughput (tokens/second)
    • Minimize latency
    • Maintain accuracy

Inference Optimization

Quantization

► Quantization: Overview
Quantization
A Survey of Quantization Methods for Efficient Neural Network Inference:
2021. http://arxiv.org/abs/2103.13630.
Reduce numerical precision of weights and activations (e.g., FP32 → INT8 → INT4)
4× smaller memory (FP32 → INT8), 8× (FP32 → INT4)
Faster operations on specialized hardware
Lower power consumption
Lower precision

Key distinctions

  • Weight-only vs. weight+activation quantization
  • From Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) to Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)
  • Symmetric vs. asymmetric quantization
  • Per-tensor vs. per-channel quantization

Challenges

  • Outliers: few extreme values dominate scale
  • Per-layer sensitivity: some layers more sensitive to quantization
  • Accumulation errors: errors compound across layers
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Quantization Mathematics

Basic (de)quantization formula

  • Map floating-point to integer: xq=round(x/s)+z
    with a scale factor: s=xmax−xminqmax−qmin and z (0 when symmetric)
  • Dequantization: x^=(xq−z)×s

Multiplication

We can compute in the quantized space x^×y^=s×s′(xq−z)×(yq−z′)
For matrix multiplication Z=XY, we often use row and column specific quantizier parameters
Zij=sisj∑k(q(Xik)−zi)×(q(Ykj)−zj)
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► LLM.int8()
LLM.Int8(): 8-Bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale:
2022. http://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07339.
Solves the problem of outliers in LLMs
higher quantization precision at scales beyond 1B parameters
explicitly represent the sparse but systematic large magnitude outlier features that ruin quantization precision once they emerge in all transformer layers starting at scales of 6.7B parameters.

More in details

B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Advanced Quantization: GPTQ
Frantar, E. et al.
2022. GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers.
  • Layer-wise quantization using second-order information
  • Minimize ‖WX−W^X‖2 where X is calibration data
  • Optimal Brain Quantization: greedily (group of column-wise) quantize weights
  • Achieves 4-bit with minimal degradation
Perplexity
Speedup
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)
LLM-QAT: Data-Free Quantization Aware Training for Large Language Models:
2023. http://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17888.
  • Straight-Through Estimator (STE)
    • Forward: quantize x^=s⋅clip(round(x/s),qmin,qmax)
    • Backward: bypass quantization ∂L∂x≈∂L∂xq
      assumption: the rounding follows a uniform distribution, x^=x+ϵ⟹∇E(x+ϵ)=∇x
“As a result, we are able to distill the 7B, 13B and 30B LLaMA models with weights and KV cache quantized down to 4-bits.”

Inference Optimization

Flash Attention

► The (self)-attention bottleneck
Self-Attention is very costly
Computing the attention logits and the convex combination
Time complexity O(d×n2) (inner product and convex combination)
GPUs are memory-bound
Compute-bound
Time = how fast the processor runs
Memory-bound
Time = how fast the memory can feed the processor
For GPUs, the gap has increased over time. See the list of Nvidia graphics processing units
Memory-intensive operations (ReLU) are memory-bound!
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Flash Attention: How GPUs work

GPU = A set of Streaming Multiprocessor

  • Each Streaming Multiprocessor is independent and has access to a fast SRAM (128-256 Ko)
  • Access to the memory is cached (L2)
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Flash Attention: core principles
FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness:
2022. http://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135.
FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning:
2023. http://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08691.
Squeeze out most of the GPU processing power

Main idea = squeeze out most of the GPU processing power

Leverage the bottleneck HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory) and SRAM (on-chip)
Fuse multiple operators in one kernel
  • Fused kernel: compute attention without materializing full matrix
  • Standard attention: O(n2) memory for attention scores
    Flash Attention: O(n) memory, faster on modern GPUs
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Flash Attention: Linear Transformation

Fuse the operations

We can compute (SRAM) Sn:p,n′:p′=Qn:p,∙K∙,n:p⊤
But how to compute sm(QK⊤)V ⁉️
For one token (over N), o=∑i=1Nexp⁡(si−m)∑jexp⁡(sj−m)vi with m=maxjsj
Posing mi=maxj≤isj, wi=∑j≤iexp⁡(sj−mi)vj, and li=∑exp⁡(sj−mi)
wi+1=emi−mi+1wi+esi+1−mi+1vi+1 and li+1=emi−mi+1li+esi+1−mi+1
(iterating over blocks rather than individual positions)
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Flash Attention: Conclusion

Other small things

Attention masks and dropout can be integrated in the algorithm

Reducing the memory

Do not materialize attention (i.e. do not store the score matrix sij)

Overall

Huge gains (speed AND memory)

Inference Optimization

Speculative Decoding

► Speculative Decoding
Speculative Decoding
Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding:
2023. http://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192.
Use a small "draft" model to generate candidate tokens, verify with large "target" model
  • Algorithm
    1. Draft model generates k tokens (fast)
    2. Target model scores all k tokens
    3. Accept tokens that match target model's distribution
    4. Resample if mismatch, continue from there
  • Properties
    • Lossless: same output distribution as target model
    • Speedup when draft model is accurate enough
    • Typical: 2-3× faster with small draft model
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Speculative Decoding: Formalization

Speculative sampling

Let p(t) and q(t) be the two distributions over tokens
We follow these steps (inspired by rejection-sampling)
  1. Sample t∼q(t)
  2. Accept the sample with a probability max(1,p(t)q(t))
  3. Resample from a probability p′(t)∝max(0,p(t)−q(t))
This is equivalent to sampling t∼p(t)
This shows we can sample from q!
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Speculative Decoding: Analysis

Expected number of generated tokens

E(# generated tokens )=1−αγ+11−α
with α=E(β) where β is the probability of accepting a token and γ the length of the sequence sampled from q
α=DLK(p,q)=∑tmin(p(t),q(t))

Expected improvement (wall time)

With c the ratio of time between inferring p and q
1−αγ+1(1−α)(γc+1)
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Speculative Decoding: Conclusion

Empirical results

Conclusion

Wall-time computation improves
Computation cost increases
Needs a good matching pair of models

Efficient & Scalable Architectures

Mixture of Experts

► Mixture of Experts (MoE)
Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity:
2022. http://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961.
Mixture of Experts
Replace dense FFN layers with multiple "expert" networks, route each token to subset of experts
  • Architecture
    • Router network: learns to assign tokens to experts
    • k experts selected per token (e.g., k=2 out of 128)
    • Only activated experts compute gradients
  • Sparse routing
    • Top-k routing: select k experts with highest scores
    • Gating function: y=∑i∈top-kgi(x)Ei(x)
    • Expert capacity: load balancing to prevent overload
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Mixture of Experts (MoE)

Wait... why this does improve things?

Each expert is assigned to a device...
and has a bounded capacity
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► MoE: Training & Inference Challenges

Training challenges

Load imbalancing: some experts overused, others ignored
Add auxiliary loss to encourage balanced routing:
∑i=1Nfi⋅∑jP(i|j) with fi the fraction of tokens dispatched to i and P(i|j) the probability that the jth token is assigned to expert i
Expert collapse: experts become redundant
Chi, Z. et al.
2022. On the Representation Collapse of Sparse Mixture of Experts.
Use a much lower-dimensional vector space for experts
Use cosine rather than inner product (to compute the expert-token match)

Benefits

  • Sparse computation: only small fraction of parameters active
  • Scale to trillions of parameters (e.g., Switch Transformer)
  • Better quality per FLOP than dense models
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3

Efficient & Scalable Architectures

Long-Range Transformers

► Long-Range Transformers: Motivation
Goal
Handle longer sequences efficiently (beyond 2K-8K tokens)
The O(n2) problem
  • Standard attention: every token attends to all others
  • Memory: O(n2), Computation: O(n2d)

Solutions

  • Linear / Kernel Approximations
  • Compressing attention heads
  • Reducing the input length
  • Hierarchical Attention
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Key-Value (KV) Cache
KV Cache
Store computed key and value vectors from previous tokens to avoid recomputation
  • Mechanics
    • During generation, each token attends to all previous tokens
    • Recomputing K, V for all past tokens is wasteful
    • Cache stores: K1:t(ℓ)=K(ℓ)x1:t(ℓ), V1:t=V(ℓ)x1:t(ℓ) for each layer
  • Memory requirements
    • Per token: 2×nlayers×dmodel (for K and V)
    • For 1000 tokens, 40 layers, 4096 dim: ~1.3GB (FP16)
    • Dominates memory for long sequences
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Low Rank and Kernel approximations: Linformer
Wang, S. et al.
2020. Linformer: Self-Attention with Linear Complexity.
The self-attention matrix P is low rank (k): P≈Plow =∑i=1kσiuiviT=[u1,⋯,uk]⏟diag{σ1,⋯,σk}[v1⋮vk]}k
Relies on the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma:
But this is even more costly ⁉️

Proposed solution: project RN×d into a Rk×d

headi―=Attention(QWiQ,EiKWiK,FiVWiV)=softmax(QWiQ(EiKWiK)Tdk)⏟P¯:n×k⋅FiVWiV⏟k×d,
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Low Rank and Kernel approximations: Performer
Choromanski, K. et al.
2020. Rethinking Attention with Performers.
Based on kernel approximations, i.e. exp⁡(x⋅y)=Eω∼N(0;Id)(ϕω(x)⋅ϕω(y)) with ϕω(x)=exp⁡(−‖x‖22)exp⁡(ω⊤x)
Hence the softmax can be approximated by
Eω∼N(0;Id)(∑jϕω(q)⊤ϕω(kj)vj)Eω∼N(0;Id)(∑jϕω(q)⊤ϕω(kj))
When using m (≈) samples (ω), the Performer self-attention becomes O(Nmd) – instead of O(N2d)
More tricks in the paper (e.g. how to better sample ω)
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Low Rank and Kernel approximations

Transformers don’t just need fast attention — they need precise attention

  • Softmax gives:
    • Scale invariance
    • Implicit competition between tokens
    • Stable gradients
  • Kernel attention often:
    • Loses normalization
    • Requires ad-hoc rescaling
    • Produces unstable attention mass

In short

kernel-based approaches breaks “sharp attention”
much better alternatives relying on exact and hierarchical attention
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► KV Cache Optimization
  • Multi-Query Attention (MQA)
    Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head Is All You Need:
    2019. http://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02150.
    • Share K, V across all attention heads
    • Only Q is multi-headed
    • Reduces KV cache size by factor of nheads
  • Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
    GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints:
    2023. http://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245.
    • Compromise: group heads, share K, V within groups
    • Example: 32 Q heads, 8 KV heads (4 heads per group)
    • Better quality than MQA, still reduces cache
  • Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)
    DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model:
    2024. http://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434.
    • Compress into a lower-dimensional latent space (much less than 2×dh×nh)
    • Shared key/value space
    • Better quality than GQA

    • Comparing the different attention mechanisms

B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3

► Reduce the input length: Compressed memory
How to increase the perception field in transformers without increasing the training cost (too much)?
Transformer-XL
Dai, Z. et al.
2019. Transformer-XL: Attentive Language Models Beyond a Fixed-Length Context.
Memory = M previous steps before the context; uses "stop-gradient" to learn
Use relative position embeddings to cater for longer contexts

► Reduce the input length: Compressed memory
Transformer-XL still limited
it keeps a fixed-length memory of past segment activations...
but eventually drops old states once memory fills up.
The Compressive Transformer improves this by maintaining two memory buffers:
Rae, J.W. et al.
2019. Compressive Transformers for Long-Range Sequence Modelling.
Different strategies are considered:
Compression function (1) max/mean pooling; (2) 1D (dilated-)convolution; (3) most-used (average attention)
Loss Reconstruction or Attention-based Reconstruction

► Reduce the input length

Conclusion

Longer range than vanilla transformers
Still limited range
Hard to train

Alternative

sparse: simpler alternatives that work well
hierarchical: allow long span and precise information fetching

Slide
► Reduce the input length: Sparse Attention Patterns
  • Local (sliding window) attention
    • Each token attends to fixed-size neighborhood (w tokens)
    • Complexity: O(n⋅w) where w≪n
    • Captures local context (like CNN)
  • Strided (dilated) attention
    • Attend to every k-th token (k=2,4,8,…)
    • Provides longer-range connections with gaps
    • Like dilated convolutions
  • Global attention
    • Few special tokens attend to all positions
    • All tokens attend to these global tokens
    • Example: CLS token, summary tokens
  • Random attention
    • Random subset of positions per token
    • Provides unexpected long-range connections
    • Helps information flow

Slide
► Reduce the input length: Sparse Attention Patterns (2)
Longformer
Beltagy, I. et al.
2020. Longformer: The Long-Document Transformer.
RoBERTa-based model that combines local windowed attention with task-specific global attention
  • All tokens: local sliding window (window size w=512)
  • Selected tokens: global attention (e.g., CLS, question tokens)
  • Complexity: O(n⋅w) instead of O(n2)
BigBird
Zaheer, M. et al.
2020. Big Bird: Transformers for Longer Sequences.
Sparse attention combining local, global, and random connections
Adds random attention to Longformer
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Hierarchical Attention: Reformer
Kitaev, N. et al.
2020. Reformer: The Efficient Transformer. ICLR.

Key idea

The problem of finding nearest neighbors quickly in high-dimensional spaces can be solved by locality-sensitive hashing (LSH)
In practive, random projections along ω: 1(ω⋅x≥0)
Allows to handle long spans (depending on the number of buckets)
Having balanced buckets is not easy, bucketing can be harmful (blurs attention – related to Performer problems)
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Hierarchical Attention: Sinkhorn
Tay, Y. et al.
2020. Sparse Sinkhorn Attention.

Key idea

Replace discrete LSH sorting with a differentiable, soft permutation of queries and keys:
  1. Sinkhorn normalization + Gumbel-Softmax to get a permutation matrix approximation
  2. Block-level reordering (not token level)
Sinkhorn normalization
A permutation matrix is a special case of a doubly stochastic matrix (rows/columns sum to 1)
Sinkhorn Normalization = a doubly stochastic matrix S(R) can be constructed from a non-negative R
Gumbel Softmax
GS(X)=S(X+ϵτ) with ϵ a Gumbel distribution noise G(0,1)
GS(X) converges to a permutation matrix when τ→0
We can take the top-K blocks = SortCut scheme
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Hierarchical Attention: Native Sparse Attention
Native Sparse Attention: Hardware-Aligned and Natively Trainable Sparse Attention:
2025. http://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11089.

Three attention mechanisms

  1. Sliding attention
  2. Block-wise attention (compressed keys and values)
  3. Selected attention (using top-k blocks from previous step) – very related to SinkHorn attention
Combines compressed attention with fine-grained localisation

Leverages Flash Attention

B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Conclusion: State-of-the-Art for Long-Context Attention

What doesn't work well

  • Linear/kernel approximations (Linformer, Performer)
    • Lose attention precision and sharpness
    • Training instability, ad-hoc rescaling needed
    • Not used in production LLMs
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Conclusion: State-of-the-Art for Long-Context Attention

What works: Hierarchical + Sparse + Exact

  • Multi-level access patterns
    • Sliding window (local context)
    • Block-wise compression (coarse global view)
    • Selected blocks (fine-grained global attention)
  • Examples: Native Sparse Attention, Sinkhorn Attention
  • Key insight: Combine fast approximate selection with exact attention

KV Cache Optimization

  • Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA): compress cached states
  • GQA/MQA: share key-value heads across queries
  • Essential for handling long contexts at inference time
Modern LLMs use sparse, learnable attention patterns with exact computation where it matters

Efficient & Scalable Architectures

Model Compression

► Model Distillation: Overview
Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network:
2015. http://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531.

Why Distillation?

  • Large models are powerful but resource-intensive
  • Distillation transfers knowledge from a large "teacher" model to a smaller "student" model
  • Enables deployment on resource-constrained devices

How to align

  • Soft labels (probabilities) from the teacher
  • Intermediate representations (features, attention maps)
  • Task-specific objectives
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Case Study: Distilling BERT to DistilBERT
Sanh, V. et al.
2019. DistilBERT, a Distilled Version of BERT: Smaller, Faster, Cheaper and Lighter.
Teacher
BERT-based (12 layers, 110M parameters)
Student
DistilBERT (6 layers, 66M parameters – 40% smaller) initialized by taking one layer out of two
Distillation loss
L=αLMLM+(1−α)LKD where LMLM is the cross-entropy loss on masked language modeling, and LKD is the Kullback-Leibler divergence between student and teacher outputs with temperature T: pi=exp⁡(zi/T)∑jexp⁡(zj/T)
Retains 97% of BERT's performance on GLUE benchmark
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Details on MiniLMv2 Distillation
A relation r is Q-Q, K-K or V-V (queries, keys or values)
Divide the teacher/student space into A parts of dimension dteacher/Ar and dstudent/Ar
The keys, values and attention maps are computed, concatenated and then split into Ar parts. Noting x(i,ℓ,a)(m) the keys/values/attention maps of token i at layer l, part a for the model m (student or teacher), we can get the similarity distribution of each part p(…|i,ℓ,a,m)=softmaxj(x(j,ℓ,a)(m)⋅x(i,ℓ,a)(m))
And then we can compute the KL between teacher and student (for layers ℓ and ℓ′, for a given relation r) Lr=1N×Ar∑a=1Ar∑i=1NKL(p(…|i,ℓ,a,m=teacher),p(…|i,ℓ′,a,m=student))

Performance

  • Retains over 95% of BERT's performance on GLUE benchmark
  • Significantly faster inference times
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide
► Distillation: Practical Considerations
  • Benefits
    • Very effective way to train smaller models
    • Used for encoders (DistilBERT) and decoders (DistilGPT-2)
    • Can match or exceed performance of training from scratch
  • Challenges
    • Requires access to teacher model during training
    • Not trivial to train – requires careful tuning
    • Temperature and loss weight balancing critical
  • Alternatives
    • Quantization: simpler, often more effective for deployment
    • Training smaller models from scratch with better data
    • Hybrid approaches: distillation + quantization
B. Piwowarski / LLMs - Efficient LLMs / Lecture 3
Slide

Conclusion

► Key Takeaways
  • Adaptation
    • PEFT methods enable efficient task-specific tuning
    • LoRA is the current standard for most applications
  • Inference optimization
    • Quantization and KV cache are critical for deployment
    • Speculative decoding offers lossless speedup
  • Efficient architectures
    • MoE enables massive scaling with sparse computation
    • Better positional encodings extend context length
    • Attention mechanism have evolved: Flash Attention + sparse and hierarchical attention
